newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil deficit cuts face fight in Congress, courts.
newsitem.headline: Brazil deficit cuts face fight in Congress, courts.

text.p: A package of measures to cut Brazil's federal spending and raise more taxes must overcome an expected barrage of opposition in the courts and in Congress before it can start to narrow the deficit, analysts said.

Ministers unveiled on Friday over 40 measures, including the aim of axing nearly 200,000 jobs, bolstering the tax service and the sale of non-operational assets of state firms, to keep the 1997 operational deficit below 2.5 percent of GDP.
But observers said the government may be exagerrating the plan's deficit-cutting potential to appease critics and improve President Fernando Henrique Cardoso's chances for re-election.
"It's a bold outline which will be difficult to put into practice...The government wants to show that it is doing something," said Dany Rappaport of MCM Consultores.

Rappaport said it was unlikely the government would recover the two billion reais it claims it will gain in 1997 by winning outstanding court cases against tax dodgers and renegotiating leases to earn more rent from its properties.
"They say they going to sack 100,000 federal government workers (and 90,000 in state companies) but are there really that many people doing nothing? It's all a little bit exagerrated," he said.

Unions lost no time in preparing for battle against the package. The Federal Public Workers Union, representing 560,000 federal workers, told its lawyers to begin preparing court challenges and was due to discuss a possible general strike along with the powerful Single Union Confederaion (CUT). The civil service unions also enjoy a strong lobby in Congress.
"This package won't reduce the deficit..., it smashes workers' rights, hits public services and fuels unemployment," said Luiz Bicalho, the union's secretary.

Eduardo Gianetti, a politics professor at Sao Paulo University, saw the package as the latest of a string of pledges to tackle Brazil's stubborn operational deficit which is this year heading for 3.5 percent of GDP this year, one percentage point higher than had been hoped.
"There are probably more details this time around but it's still going to involve drawn out negotiations to turn it into reality," Gianetti said.
Regardless of the package, the government will come under pressure in 1997 to award civil servants a pay rise after their salaries were frozen this year.

However, one indirect effect of the measures may be to help get through Congress a constitutional amendment that would allow Cardoso the chance of re-election. "Politicians will be looking to link their support for re-election to their objections (to the package)," Gianetti said.
